utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday we were dealing with the motion in limine raised by Mr. Zecevic, and we were about to hear the Prosecution's response, or rather, reply. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Defence counsel has filed what would appear to be a motion in limine, requesting that we omit certain pieces of evidence of certain testimony before this Chamber. Three areas of evidence: one, evidence concerning Milan Simic's activities prior to assuming the position of executive -- of president of the Executive Board, which was at the end of May he assumed that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May 1992, I believe May 30th. Any activity they want to have us be precluded from introducing. The second issue is evidence concerning a rape or sexual assault committed by Milan Simic in late August of 1992 in Bosanski Samac. The third issue is evidence of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [redacted]--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Not the name, just the description. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: A Muslim female.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Not the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What were the circumstances, according to the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: According to the Prosecution's case, the victim had known the next witness. The next witness was a practicing attorney in Bosanski Samac, a very well-respected resident of Bosanski Samac. The victim and the next witness were both sent to Zasavica. One week after the rape, the victim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When you say they were both sent to Zasavica, was this a camp or was it as part of the -- what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Zasavica was kind of a -- I'd say a peninsula or type area -- it was an area where there was one entrance. It was kind of in the shape of a U, where there was one entrance to enter. The people were told that it was mined all around the area, and you could not get out of the entrance because there were guards. Women, elderly men, Croatian men, who were younger, mostly elderly Muslim men, Croatian and Muslim women, were held there as prisoners. The women whose husbands had escaped, whose husbands were being imprisoned, whose husbands had escaped and were fighting on the other side, were held. Women, children, elderly, and there were a small number of younger men, mainly Croatian, that were -- and a few younger Muslim men that were held there, for whatever reasons. There were some farms there and they were required to maintain the farms, and the rest of the people lived there, performed forced labour, but they just took over other people's homes. It was a very beautiful -- you'll hear testimony that it was a very beautiful little village where there were farms and a church, and it was just taken over and it was used as a prison camp. During her first few days in Zasavica, this witness is approached by the victim. The victim tells her about a rape that was committed a week prior by Milan Simic. The victim was - I'm sorry - the witness was kind of surprised, because the witness was kind of like a second mother, was known as aunt to Milan, and she tells him the facts. What had happened was, one week prior, 80 to 100 Muslim men had escaped the Bosanski Samac area. They swam across the river. This was one of the large escapes which occurred. The wives and families of all of those people who escaped were imprisoned in Zasavica within the following week. The night of the escape, Milan Simic visits this person, 2.30 in the morning, with a friend. They get her out of her home. He's taken to her friend's house -- I'm sorry, the friend of -- or the cohort of Milan Simic, and the rape occurs. She is held for the night and she is returned the next morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: To the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. That's to her house or her friend's house where she was staying. Two days later, she's placed in Zasavica with all the other families of the persons who escaped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So the rape occurred to the victim before she was taken to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Two days prior being taken to the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But after her husband had escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On the evening of the husband escaped in the late evening, between 3.00 and 7.00 in the morning the rape occurred. Now, what -- in addressing that issue, we are not addressing any evidence of an extramarital affair. There's actually two pieces of evidence, if I could go back to the facts. What then happens, approximately three weeks later, a group of women are in the victim's house in Zasavica. A car stops, the defendant and his friend exit the car and walk right into the house. He's surprised to see his aunt there basically, "What are you doing there?" "No, why don't you tell me what you're doing here?" They have some conversation, they're there for 30 minutes and then they leave. I would want to bring in certainly that conversation which occurred. It doesn't involve the rape, but the fact that he's just showing up inside of a prison camp in the evening in the victim's house walking in just opening the door and walking in with his friend is corroborative. But what I want to do here is introduce this evidence for -- and I'm arguing that it is relevant for several areas for many reasons. One, this defendant has been charged with crimes against humanity. As the Court knows for a crime against humanity, we have to prove that the crimes were widespread and systematic, widespread and systematic against civilians. These incidents, the incidents of rape, torture, beatings, killings, which were committed by Milan Simic, allegedly committed by Milan Simic and/or several other persons are all evidence of the widespread nature of the attack which occurred against the citizens of Bosanski Samac and Odzak. These incidents are also proof of his power and authority in Bosanski Samac. This is proof how he is able to enter a prison camp, whether it's the prison camp where the Bicic brothers were or the Zasavica. He had the power and authority to enter that camp. He's had the power and authority to go into houses and remove people. He's had the power to remove prisoners at later times and there will be other proof of removing this same woman right after this witness leaves Zasavica and is exchanged. Evidence that he goes back. This evidence is also corroborative. It's corroborative of the Bicic brothers, and it's corroborative in the area of Rule 93. Rule 93 allows us to introduce a pattern of conduct to prove an issue. What does this show? Late night visit, just like with the Bicics; accompanied by others, just like with the Bicics; removing prisoners or removing persons from their temperate residence or some residence, just like the Bicics; harming local people, just like the Bicics incident and other incidents. There will be other testimony of late night visits, and harming local people who were not Serbs, a discriminatory intent. Now, we are going to hear evidence of June with the Bicics, another witness will be the first witness after the break to testify, Mr. Hadzialijagic, of a July incident. You're are going to hear about this incident, which is an August incident, all of these late-night incidents where the defendant enters a prison camp. Now, in a recent decision, in the Kvocka decision, a recent issue was raised at pages 155 and 156 in the Kvocka decision. One of the co-defendants was charged with all sorts of actions and one witness testifies apparently for the first time that she was raped at paragraph 554, 554. Witness AT testified that Radic called her out of her room several times during her 23 days spent in Omarska camp like other women, she was taken to a room at the end of the corridor where a sponge mattress was on the floor. The witness described how, on one such occasion, Radic told her to take her clothes off and forced her to have sexual intercourse with him. Now, on page 556, the Court notes that these were not -- this rape was not indicted. This is not part of the amended indictment, but the court says, "The testimony of Witness AT charging Radic with rape will not, therefore, be considered in the determination of his guilt. However, the Trial Chamber is satisfied that the testimony of this witness is highly credible and can assist in establishing a consistent pattern of conduct in conformity with Rule 93." And that's what we're trying to do. One of the bases is to establish this consistent pattern of conduct which bolsters the testimony of other witnesses and corroborates the testimony of other witnesses. In another way this evidence is admissible, under the Kordic judgement, the recent Kordic judgement from February of this year. In that case the Court mentions three levels of then mental state of mens rea. One, the government must prove a discriminatory intent; two, there must be an intent to commit the act, the criminal act; and three, a general intent of knowledge of a widespread and systematic attack against Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. civilians. These acts prove hostility towards non-Serb civilians. It shows an intent to act, that these weren't accidental. The way I'm guessing their Defence is going to be, the attack on the Bicic brothers and Perica Mesic and Ibrahim Salkic was a situation when he was drunk. These situations -- these pieces of evidence show that this was a persistent type of conduct that was committed against the Bicics in June, against Hadzialijagic in July, against this woman in August. That these were intentional actions committed by this defendant. And further, from his involvement in various types of crimes, from his visits to prison camps including this act, his knowledge of the widespread nature of the attack against civilians can be inferred. So what we would like to do is not prove that he committed the rape. Rape is not a charge here. We want to use this evidence to prove the widespread and systematic attack against the civilians, his knowledge, his intent, use it for corroboration, use it to show a certain pattern of conduct which corroborates what the other witnesses will say. And for those reasons, it is our argument based on the judgements of this Court and its relevance that this evidence should be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. Anything in response?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First of all, we made the motion in limine yesterday, but we still say that this evidence is not relevant because if it hasn't been alleged in the indictment or if it had been alleged, actually, in the indictment, it would be relevant, but there are no legal nor factual allegations of sexual assault nor exchanges against Milan Simic. The statement of the witness says "a sexual encounter," the statement which was disclosed to us. The Rule 93(B) says, "Acts tending to show such a pattern of conduct shall be disclosed by the Prosecutor to the Defence pursuant to Rule 66." Your Honours, the Defence and the defendant has been taken by surprise just yesterday when we received this summary, and it is our understanding that for the sake of the fairness in the trial, the surprise should never work against the defendant. The surprise should never work against the defendant. And what my learned colleague was alleging over here during his speech just now is that he's trying to create the pattern and then he is using some - I don't know - things which are really not a part of the case. Actually, we have heard the Bicic brothers, and they say that Milan Simic came only once and that Safet Hadzialijagic allegedly was beaten the same night, and not in July, Your Honours, and that is why we really think that this is completely unfair and we are still pursuing our motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I think we heard from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just one matter. Just one thing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. One minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Not even one minute. I just want to read the line from the initial discovery. Not the recent discovery yesterday; the initial discovery: "From 3.00 a.m. until 7.00 a.m., she had to do all kinds of sexual performance with Milan Simic." They've had discovery about this sexual incident and other sexual incidents. I can read -- there are others here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When was that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One moment, please. This is a 1998 statement, and I'll give you the date of filing discovery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Whose statement is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's the statement of this witness here, our next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Witness K?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We believe it was filed in discovery in February of 1999. I can give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just want to be sure: That is the statement of Witness K?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. February 23rd, 1999, it was given to them in discovery, over two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, but this statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This statement doesn't say anything about the sexual assault. It does refer to the sexual encounter between -- alleged sexual encounter between my client and the third party, which is deleted altogether, her -- and he was never charged in the indictment for the sexual assault, nor is there any allegation, factual or legal, about the sexual assault, not even in a part of the article which deals with the persecution. This was not mentioned in the indictment. Therefore, we really believe that the motion in limine should be granted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. As this matter affects the next witness, the Judges will retire to consider this matter so that it can be -- the motion can be decided before the witness starts to give evidence. So the Court will rise. --- Break taken at 9.54 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has considered the motion in limine raised by the Defence counsel for Mr. Milan Simic. It has also considered the submissions by both parties, especially the submissions by both the Prosecution and the Defence in that the statement of the witness making sexual allegations was served on the Defence and therefore there is no surprise element. The Trial Chamber is of the view that there was sufficient disclosure, especially the fact that rape is not charged -- is not being charged as a separate charge against Mr. Milan Simic, and the Trial Chamber finds that in the interests of justice, the evidence of this witness along the lines mentioned by the Prosecution should be allowed. Therefore, the motion in limine is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I have one minute just to confer with my client and my co-counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, just for the purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is for the position of the Defence that to allow the Prosecution to present evidence regarding sexual assaults and exchanges violates the defendant's right to due process of law. One of the most fundamental rights of the defendant has to be is that the defendant has to be given notice of the charges against him. There are no allegations of sexual assault or deportation in the indictment. These are both separate and distinct crimes under the Statute of this Tribunal. If the Prosecution wants to present the evidence against this defendant, they should have given the defendant notice in the indictment. Rule 47(B) and (C) says that if there is a sufficient evidence that a suspect committed a crime, the Prosecutor shall prepare an indictment for confirmation along with supporting material. It shall set forth a concise statement of the facts. The defendant has not been presented with charges of these alleged crimes and being denied the right to enter a plea on these charges. More importantly, the defendant has not been -- has been denied the right to defend against these charges because there was no notice of the allegations. There are -- Your Honours, in our motion in limine, there were three distinct matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic. You don't have to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We already heard that. I've given you leave to say what you want to say for the sake of the record, fine. So you don't have -- we are not going back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know, Your Honours, we are not going back but I -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And there is no --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand has this ruling been on all three?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On all three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, however, it is our position that the Prosecutor is bringing new charges against our client and then we ask the Prosecutor to amend the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's all?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. There is nothing that the Defence counsel has raised that will move the Trial Chamber to decide otherwise. The Prosecution will call their witness and call the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour. There's another matter Ms. Reidy, just a very brief matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, it's a very brief matter. In fact, if the usher would like to get the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we go ahead, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes. It's just yesterday there was some discussion on the record by Defence of Prosecution Exhibit P41 ter, and they said that it had not been disclosed to them, and Mr. Zecevic said he knew it hadn't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. been disclosed because that document had no ERN number. It was disclosed on the 8th of February of this year. We have signed receipts for that of which I have given copies to the Defence. It was, in fact, put on the record at the Status Conference of the same date of the 8th of February, 2001 that the disclosure had been made, and I just put it on the record because again, Mr. Lukic, on behalf of his client, had asked to re-examine on that document because he had no notice of it. I know there was change of counsel. I'm not -- he himself personally might not have seen it, but there are signed statements for the 8th of February, and it was all part of the Status Conference that the Prosecution had fully complied with their disclosure obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I have confirmation from the Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In fact, Madam President, yes, it is true that our learned friends provided us with the sort of list of the documents, but the problem is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, with that particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, with this particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. You heard what Ms. Reidy said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard, and I just want to inform this Trial Chamber that there was no specification of the actually contents of this bunch of documents of 25 pages, and to the best of my knowledge, I'm speaking, I think, on behalf of all my colleagues but specifically on behalf of my client, there is no -- and acceptable evidence that all these -- actually, the document in question was included in this bunch of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So what you are saying, Mr. Pantelic, that that particular document, it's Exhibit P41 ter, was not served on the Defence. That is your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is my position, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is that the position, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I stated yesterday that this is the first time I have seen this document so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, that is the position, it was not served as alleged by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before my cross-examination, once I received the document from my colleague, Mr. Pisarevic, and we are talking about documents which I presented during the cross-examination, I discussed them with my colleague, Ms. Reidy, from the Prosecution. At that moment, she, too, was unable to confirm that the documents had been served and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, the point is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are talking about document P41. I hadn't seen it and I talked to a representative of the OTP about documents that I will show the witness. She confirmed that we had received the documents but not the indictment. I hadn't seen document P41 until it was introduced in the redirect examination by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, is that the same with you that you were never served with P41?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my position is the following: Basically, I support what my colleagues have said because I did receive the documents that are mentioned but there was no specification and document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So when you saw that document, your position is that you've never received such a document. That is the question I'm asking. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The indictment --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- under number P41 is a document which I have never received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Call the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. Please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, please sit on the chair provided. Yes, the Prosecution can go ahead. Examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you look at this piece of paper in front of you, please. We're going to be referring to you as Witness K for this trial. You'll notice on that sheet of paper there are the letters A, B, and C. Beside the letter A, there is a name. Is that your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Beside the letter B is a date of birth. Is that your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, it's the correct date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And beside letter C is the name of a city or a municipality. Is that the municipality where you were born?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, we, again, have a problem. The clients are not hearing anything in the -- in their earphones and also, we never received this piece of paper, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Can we check first with the channel for the accused persons. But can counsel hear the witness? Can you hear -- with the Defence counsel, can you hear the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was listening without my earphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: On what channel are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm on the English channel, number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So they are supposed to be on what channel?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters also have troubles hearing the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The interpreters are also saying they have trouble hearing the witness. Let's wait -- I want to make sure that the accused persons can hear the proceedings. Is it still the same problem, nothing? Still the same problem, nothing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, what they are saying is that they don't know until the witness starts talking, because the problem is they don't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. Can we have the number of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution document P42, and the document is under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It will be under seal. Yes, under seal. Can you just greet the witness until we get the confirmation from the accused persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can the witness count to 5?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the witness please count to 5 to see if their microphones are working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see that it's not working. They can't get the witness. We'll just wait for the technical people. Can we test?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the witness please count to 5 again and we'll see if all of the earphones are working.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's on channel 7, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Weiner, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And remember always to switch off your mike after asking the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend high school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you graduate high school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: In Samac, in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of high school was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: It was the high school for economics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go on for further education after you received your high school degree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: The first level of law at university.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you attend law school? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you practice law after graduation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, not as an attorney, but I did work as a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court where you worked as a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I worked in the organisation of eight associations of self-interest communities in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these government agencies at the municipal level?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, at the municipal level. I worked in an institution that was at the regional level also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you work as a lawyer for the government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: For four and a half years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that, what job did you have and where did you work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I worked in the self -- in the interest community of health insurance for 15 or 16 years, and I passed through all the various units of this organisation, and for a little under a year I worked as a lawyer. So I was a cashier, I was an officer in charge of insurance for people working abroad, then of insurance for employees, and then self-management.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the 15 to 16 years that you worked in this government agency, did you handle or prepare any sort of financial paperwork?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Well, yes. There was also a financial part of my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you said you weren't an attorney, you were a lawyer, in Bosnia an attorney is a private practicing person and a lawyer is the attorney -- if you want to call it, the person who works for the government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you own any property in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you own a business in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of business?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever a guest of honour at any political party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For which party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: The SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were you their guest of honour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Before the party had formally been established, at the outset, I didn't have a membership card or anything, because I gave up on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were a guest of honour at a meeting of the SDA, did you join that party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or join any other party, political party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of what nationality are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I'm Bosniak by nationality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of what religion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: By birth, I should belong to the Islamic faith, but I'm an atheist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever owned a firearm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No. I personally never owned one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having lived in Bosanski Samac, I'm going to ask you to look around the room and ask if you see anybody in this courtroom that you might recognise. First, have you ever known a man by the name of Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had you known Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Well, before the war, Mr. Simic graduated from the medical school and worked in our health centre. He was a charming and a nice man, very dear to me, and when he became president of the Serbian Democratic Party, I congratulated him on being elected to that function, with Mitar Trifunovic. I hadn't known him for long, but my opinion of him was high.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look around the courtroom, and could you just tell me, yes or no, is he in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: He's in the courtroom, sitting next to Milan Simic. He has a beard, his hair is receding. What else can I say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I've known Miroslav Tadic, if we take into account these ten years that I've been away from Bosanski Samac, or Samac, as it is called today, for 30 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look around the courtroom and tell the Court whether Miroslav Tadic is in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: He is indeed. His hair is greying. He has spectacles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does he have anything on his face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: He has a moustache. I don't see very well. I need eyeglasses to see far. I can't see details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you look around and tell us whether he is in this courtroom at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, he is. On the left of Mr. Blagoje Simic. He is wearing eyeglasses, he's wearing a tie and black shirt with a pepita jacket. I think the shirt is black. I don't see that well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, do you know a man by the name of Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I know him very well. I used to love him more than my own son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did Milan Simic refer to you and your husband?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he refer to you, did he address you in some way, you and your husband?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Milan Simic in the courtroom at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us where he's seated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: He is the first in the row, the most handsome of them all. He's wearing a jacket. I believe it's a sports jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the record reflect that all four defendants have been identified by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: husband was getting ready to go to work. He was doing the night shift in the Energopetrol company and, panic stricken, he got into his car and drove away [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: [redacted]. When it was all over, we went back home and the police remained to secure the building. Among them was the police commander, Savo Cancarevic, until the morning when fire experts, technicians from Doboj came.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: [redacted] Soldiers coming from Croatia used this road and they often threw away, discarded their helmets, their weapons, et cetera. My son brought it home and his father reprimanded him for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just very briefly, you had a problem in March of 1992 [redacted].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what date did you have that problem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: On the 9th, in the morning around 3.00, but before 4.00 in the morning. I can't be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: [redacted]. I put on a raincoat over my nightgown and went straight there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: [redacted] the police officers were extremely decent. They were waiting again for the fire technicians from Doboj to arrive, and I have to say this about Mr. Savo Cancarevic, he deserves a lot of credit as well as Djoko Mascic. They were very sympathetic [redacted] [redacted].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: [redacted]. I don't know how else to explain it. That's how this episode ended to my great joy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us just discuss a few things briefly. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of the information you received from the private detective and [redacted] did you do something?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyway, I called him on the telephone to ask him for an interview and we agreed to meet in a pizzeria owned by Hasan or Muhamed Bicic. Sometime between 3.00 and 4.00 we, indeed, met up and we talked. I wanted to remind Simo of who I was and why all that was happening to me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what date did you meet with Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That was the 9th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you ask him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I asked Simo Zaric to spare me for all the -- from all the unpleasantness that was happening to me and to explain why it was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell him the results of the investigation and who had committed the [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you ask him in specific -- as best as you can recall the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I asked him to be spared from all the dirty business, as I saw it. My husband was a member of the SDA, and when this [redacted]happened, I didn't think it was a political incident, I thought it was inspired by jealousy, rather. I'm a very hard working woman, very hard working entrepreneur who continued in a regular job while engaging in private business. And when I talked to Bogolub, for instance, he said, "Do you know which nationality I am?" I said, "I'm not interested in that. I got your name [redacted] [redacted]. And we don't discriminate against people according to their colour or race or ethnic background. In my view, you are a good expert." When he indicated that this might be a political incident, I rejected that suggestion because I thought it was more likely to be revenge. And while talking to that detective, I realised that political games were going on all around me, although I was not part of them. And when I talked to Simo, I asked him to remember what kind of family I come from. I asked him to remember that Yugoslavia was created by families like mine, and from my own family, 29 people gave their lives for our country. And when I talked to Simo, I told him that I would get my own weapon. Please allow me to say this. And on that occasion, Simo said that was not necessary, that he would provide security [redacted], and that it was not set to harm me [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please explain to me what you mean [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted] -- the buildings are not attached to each other. There is just a narrow space between our respective premises, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted]? Was he related to a certain individual from the SDA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. It is just for a matter of clarification. The witness stated "spiceraj," and in the transcript we see "pizzeria," and these are completely different kind of businesses. I mean, maybe it's just a matter of translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: According to you, what should it have been?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is some sort of a store with mixed goods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Nothing to do with food?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Nothing to do with restaurants, pizzerias, or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Can we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What -- please continue. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I am sorry, but from childhood, I've known these stores as mixed-goods shops where you find food, toiletries and various other things. I will continue to call it a mixed-goods store rather than using the local term.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. They do not know the exact English translation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I can explain. You could find things like bacon, kajmak, sugar, cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I think we understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think it's general groceries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: A grocery store.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: A sundry shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [redacted]. He worked for a while in the electrical company, and I think that before the war -- I should say that his wife operated this sundries shop, as you said. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [redacted]. He was a member of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, because Simo and I were good friends, fellow citizens on very good terms with each other, and we had had no prior conflicts. And probably out of compassion and knowing where I come from, he said on that occasion, "You don't have to take special care of your shop. I'll take care of that. I will guard it."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after Simo Zaric assured you that he would take care of your property, up to the war, was [redacted] ever damaged or injured in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Not before the war. There was nothing left to damage or injure [sic].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the war, up to April 17th, was your property -- after Simo Zaric indicated that your property would be protected, was it damaged or harmed in any way, that piece of property or any other property that you owned, prior to April 17th?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: -- managed to convert it later and repair it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Between the meeting with Simo Zaric on March 9th, when Simo Zaric said he would protect your property, between that date and April 17th, the day of the -- that the war began, was your property harmed in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you had that conversation with Mr. Zaric about the protection of your property, was there any conversation concerning the 4th Detachment, what was it was and what it was planned to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Court. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Well, I talked to him. I was embittered [redacted], and knowing that the two perpetrators belonged to the 4th Detachment, I asked Simo what kind of organisation it was, to whom it belonged. He told me that it was established as a multi-ethnic unit. He even quoted the percentages of various ethnic groups in it. He said it was 60 per cent Serbs, 10 per cent Croats, and 30 per cent Muslims. He said it was organised to protect Bosanski Samac from all paramilitary units, and then he specified from the Arkan men, the HOS, Green Berets, and I don't know any other paramilitary formations. There were lots of them. And to that I replied, "Dear Simo, if that is so, why did you bypass my son, my house and my son?" And he said, "I bypassed you because you have only one son." And I asked him, "Maybe the reason was that his father was in the SDA. I would be glad to know that you were driven by compassion and wanted to spare my son, but I suspect there may be other reasons." Unfortunately, the 4th Detachment included many only sons who eventually got killed and whose mothers wear black to this day. They died very young.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have a break? Yes. We'll continue the proceedings at 11.30 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution is continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us move to April 16th, 1992. Did you work that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I did not work that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the day of the attack, the attack was in the early morning hours, the day preceding that, [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a busy day? It was just prior to Easter, I believe, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say no, it wasn't a busy day or it wasn't just prior to Easter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: It was before Easter, and people [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do anything as a result of having few customers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I don't understand you very, very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: [redacted], and in the afternoon after 4.00 or 5.00 or 6.00 p.m., I saw many, many people leaving, getting into vehicles with bags and there was something unusual going on so I closed the shop. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you walked home, did you notice anything about the houses in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. Samac was not lighted up and the weather was dark. There were only a few lights here and there, so everything was wrapped in darkness and even the sky was dark as if God was warning us that something that is going to happen. There were birds flying around. There was something in the atmosphere that suggested something bad was about to happen. And my fellow citizens, those who were of Serb ethnicity were moving out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got home, was anyone else in your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: My husband was at home, and I told him everything. I told him something was afoot in Samac, and when I told him that, he got dressed and went to Rustica. There he found Izetbegovic, Lukac, Sulejman Tihic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Rustica is a restaurant in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. It was owned by the late Mr. Ivo. It was a well-known restaurant where those of us who were middle aged very often met.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when your husband met with them on that evening of the 16th, did he tell them of your concerns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, he did. And then the people I have enumerated told him to go home in peace. He said, "My wife is in a panic because she saw all this. All I can see is that there are no lights. Well, there was some lights, but my wife is sensitive and she looked at where the lights were on and she made some telephone calls because there are buildings nearby where she has many friends, and in the flats where the lights were on, nobody answered the phone so this gave me a creepy feeling." He told the people in Rustica about this, but Sulejman Tihic told him that he had an agreement with Mr. Blagoje Simic and that nothing could happen, nothing bad could happen in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, later that night, did anyone visit your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, [redacted] [redacted] he said that he had received information and it concerned paramilitary units, I am not clear about which ones, was it Arkan's men or the Grey Wolves or whatever they were called. I don't want to remember these units. He said they had arrived and taken over the mill. That was the mill was a wheat-processing plant on the other side of the railway tracks, and we refer to it as the outskirts of Samac. It was two or three kilometres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as a result of him saying that to you, did your husband do anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: My husband again went to Rustika. He was even more worried now, and he told those people who were having dinner, and probably drinking too, he told them what he had been told by [redacted]. But they said to him again, "Go home and sleep quietly. We had a meeting with Mr. Blagoje Simic, and he said everything was all right in Samac and that nothing bad could happen."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you go to bed that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Maybe my husband did. I didn't look at the clock, but about an hour later my husband did go to bed. But I had a huge pile of laundry, so I started ironing, and I listened to music, to the Nedaj se Bosna, the Bosnian station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did something happen in the early morning hours of April 17th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Well, as soon as I went to bed, it was very, very late. It was maybe 2.00 a.m. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: went out onto the terrace of my house and I saw that Samac was burning. There were many explosions and many flames, and then I saw what sort of trouble we were in. We were surprised. My husband took a rifle and went out. He came back soon afterwards, in tears, and he said, "Samac has been occupied." I replied to him, "By whom?" And he said, "Soldiers are in here, the army." And I said, "Oh, that's wonderful, because they will disarm all the paramilitaries who are walking around with weapons." And I was very happy, because my uncle was in the JNA. It's true that he was a retired colonel. And I also had a relative, actually, a brother-in-law. I am the only member of my family who is married to a Muslim, and I have two brothers-in-law who are Serbs and one who is a Croat. However, in the morning I saw it was not just the JNA, and then things became very clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you try and use your telephone that evening, or during those early-morning hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The telephones had been cut off, the lights had been cut, water had been cut, and the phones had been cut. At around 11.00 a.m., my telephone line started operating again and the electricity came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 17th, from, let's say, the morning on, did you do anything that day?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you didn't stay out on the balcony. Did you do anything else on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: On that day I went out. Perhaps I was braver than my husband was. He was trembling. My son came home only 20 minutes before Samac was set on fire. He socialised with Goran Pisarevic, with Marinkovic. My son did not have any friends who are Muslims, I think. He kept company with Serbs and Croats. But that night the young Mesic, our next-door neighbour, happened to be with them, and Goran Pisarevic and all of them left Valentino, the establishment where young people went to have a drink. My son came home drunk. I tried to wake him up. I tried to leave Samac, but I at least was unable to leave Samac, because all around our house there were snipers, on all the roofs, and every attempt of mine to leave was met by a sniper shooter. I tried to go out to buy bread, more out of curiosity, because I wanted to see what was going on, and I would go back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move to the next day, April 18th. Did something happen on April 18th? Tell the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: On April the 18th, seven young men, and maybe two married men, came to the front of my house. I knew some of them well and others I saw for the first time. They --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that, did something happen? Was there anyone running Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. around in a vehicle with a megaphone, or do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, yes. The Serbian police went around. They were driving around in a vehicle. It probably belonged to our SUP. I didn't look at the licence plate. And they used a megaphone, saying that whoever had weapons should hand them over and nothing bad would happen to them. I went out and waved to the young man. He stopped. He was very polite. He looked very neat, very decent, in a uniform. He was clean-shaven. He didn't look like a paramilitary. He stopped the vehicle and he said, "Madam, what do you want?" And I said, "My husband has a rifle and I would like to hand it over." And he said, "Well, bring it out." And I said, "No. I don't dare touch the weapon." I had really never held it in my hands. So he got out of the car and he said, "Madam, where is your husband?" And I said, "Well, there he is. He's at home. He's terrified." And he said, "Well, what if your husband shoots at me?" And I said to him, as I would address my own son, I said, "Honey, I'll go first, and if my husband shoots, he'll shoot me. He has never fired shots." So he went behind me and he had his hand on my shoulder. I went in first. The rifle was in the corridor and he collected it. He asked my husband if he had any more weapons, and my husband said he didn't. The young man said, "If you do, hand them over, because there will be other people coming after me to search houses, so you'll be better off if you give it to me." And I wanted to escort the young man back to the vehicle, and he said, "No, madam." He looked up at the white building and he said, "We do have security." He was really very polite. I don't know him, but if anybody here does know him, he should convey my gratitude to him. Not long after that, seven armed people came. I knew some of them, others not. I knew Ljubo nicknamed Cigance, and I also know Dragan Borojevic. They surrounded my front door. Cigance was hiding because he was ashamed, and that Cera stood in front of my door and another man from Skarici who knew me because my weekend cottage had been in Skarici Polje. Cera was yelling and saying, "You have weapons. You have weapons." And I opened the door and said, "It's because of people like you that I have lost my weekend cottage. Come in. Search the house. If you find anything, you can kill my husband, and my son, and me." And then the tall man from Skaric, whom I didn't know, said to Cera, "Calm down, you can see that the woman has opened the gate wide but they didn't enter the house, they left."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are having problems with redactions. Can we move into private session, it's much better, because the people in the gallery can hear the witness directly. There is no time for the redaction to work so it's safer to be in the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Our request is to move into private session based on the comments then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
